title: Quantization Formats, Serving Frameworks & GPU Memory Math
scopeHtml: Scope: GPTQ/AWQ/GGUF, TGI/llama.cpp/Triton, and estimating model and inference memory.

notes.title: Bits, bytes and why formats exist
notes.html:
Start with the one fact everything else hangs on: a model is a huge pile of numbers (weights), and every number costs bytes. A parameter is one weight. "Llama 3 70B" means about 70 billion of them. If each weight is stored as a 16-bit float (fp16 or bf16, 2 bytes), the file is roughly 70e9 x 2 = 140e9 bytes = 140 GB. No single GPU holds that (an 80 GB H100 has 80 GB). Quantization means storing each weight with fewer bits (8, 4, sometimes 3 or 2) plus a small amount of extra data to map the small integers back to approximate real numbers. A 4-bit version of the same model is about 35 to 40 GB, which fits one 80 GB card with room left over.

See also: C2/notes/02_Q1.md covers the general idea of quantization (weight-only vs weight+activation, PTQ vs QAT, quality impact). This note goes one level down: the actual file formats and algorithms (GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF), the servers that run them (TGI, llama.cpp, Triton), and the arithmetic that tells you whether a model fits a GPU before you rent one.

Why are there several formats and not one? Because they solve different problems:

Format   Made for                  Typical runtime            Stored as
-------  ------------------------  -------------------------  -------------------------
GPTQ     GPU serving, 4-bit        vLLM, TGI, transformers    safetensors + quant config
AWQ      GPU serving, 4-bit        vLLM, TGI, transformers    safetensors + quant config
GGUF     CPU / Apple / mixed GPU   llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio  one single .gguf file
FP8      Hopper/Ada/Blackwell GPU  vLLM, TensorRT-LLM        safetensors

Think of the format as the packaging (how bytes sit in a file, what metadata travels with them) and the method as the recipe that decided which integers to store. GPTQ and AWQ are mainly methods that happen to have a common packaging on the Hugging Face Hub. GGUF is mainly a packaging (one file with weights, tokenizer and metadata) that comes with its own family of quantization types.

Where this appears in real life: Hugging Face model pages for popular models usually have community quantized repos with names like ...-GPTQ, ...-AWQ and ...-GGUF (publishers such as TheBloke historically, and now many others, plus the model authors themselves). Ollama's library is almost entirely GGUF under the hood. vLLM and TGI load GPTQ/AWQ checkpoints directly.

The bytes-per-weight table you should memorise (we derive the 4-bit rows later):

Precision            Bits/weight   Bytes/weight   70B model size
-------------------  -----------   ------------   --------------
fp32                 32            4              280 GB
fp16 / bf16          16            2              140 GB
int8 / fp8           8             1              70 GB
4-bit (+ scales)     ~4.2 to 4.8   ~0.53 to 0.6   ~37 to 42 GB

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: it is like saving a photo. The original RAW file (fp16) is huge. JPEG at quality 90 (8-bit) looks identical. Quality 40 (4-bit) is a fraction of the size and still looks fine unless you zoom in on fine text. Different "JPEG encoders" (GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF types) make different trade-offs about which details to protect.

Production failure pattern: a team downloads "the 70B model", sees 140 GB in the repo, and orders 2 x 80 GB GPUs thinking that is enough. The weights alone fill 140 of 160 GB, leaving nothing for the KV cache (see the memory sections), and the server dies with out-of-memory under real traffic.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "quantization makes the model smaller" without naming what is stored: low-bit integers PLUS scales/zero-points. The extra metadata is why "4-bit" really costs about 4.2 to 4.8 bits per weight.
  • Treating GPTQ, AWQ and GGUF as the same kind of thing. GPTQ and AWQ are algorithms; GGUF is a file format with its own quant types.
  • Forgetting that a quantized checkpoint is a separate artefact: you cannot flip a flag and turn a fp16 repo into a GPTQ one at load time for free (some runtimes quantize on load, like bitsandbytes or vLLM FP8, but GPTQ/AWQ need a calibration pass).

notes.title: The quantization arithmetic by hand
notes.html:
Before the named methods, learn the primitive they all build on: scale-and-round. This is the part interviewers like to check, because it is small enough to do on paper.

Step by step, for a group of weights (a small block that shares one scale):

  1. Find the largest absolute value in the group: m = max(|w|).
  2. Pick the integer range. Signed 4-bit holds -8 to 7. Using 7 as the top: scale = m / 7.
  3. Quantize each weight: q = round(w / scale), clipped to [-8, 7].
  4. Store the small integers q (4 bits each) and the one scale (fp16, 16 bits) per group.
  5. At runtime dequantize: w_hat = q * scale. The difference w - w_hat is the quantization error.

Worked example with a group of four weights [0.10, -0.42, 0.31, 0.07]:

m     = 0.42
scale = 0.42 / 7 = 0.06
q     = round([0.10, -0.42, 0.31, 0.07] / 0.06)
      = round([1.67, -7.00, 5.17, 1.17]) = [2, -7, 5, 1]
w_hat = [2, -7, 5, 1] * 0.06 = [0.12, -0.42, 0.30, 0.06]
error = [-0.02, 0.00, 0.01, 0.01]

Notice what happened: the biggest weight is exact, the small weights absorbed all the error. Now imagine a single outlier such as 4.0 sneaking into the same group: scale = 4.0/7 = 0.571, and 0.10 rounds to round(0.175) = 0, 0.07 to 0, 0.31 to round(0.54) = 1 (0.571). All the fine information is destroyed. This is the core reason for group size: smaller groups (32, 64, 128 weights) isolate outliers so one big value only ruins its own small neighbourhood. The price is more scales to store.

Overhead math (this is how you get "4.5 bits" from "4 bits"):

Group of 32, fp16 scale:   4 bits + 16/32  = 4.5 bits per weight    (llama.cpp Q4_0)
Group of 128, fp16 scale:  4 bits + 16/128 = 4.125 bits per weight
  plus a 4-bit zero-point per group of 128: + 4/128 = 4.156 bits     (typical GPTQ/AWQ g128)
Group of 32, int8:         8 bits + 16/32  = 8.5 bits per weight    (llama.cpp Q8_0)

Symmetric quantization (above) centres at zero. Asymmetric adds a zero-point so the range can be shifted (useful when weights in a group are mostly positive). GPTQ and AWQ checkpoints commonly store both scales and zero-points per group.

Python, a tiny runnable demonstration:

import numpy as np

def quant_group(w, bits=4):
    qmax = 2 ** (bits - 1) - 1              # 7 for 4-bit signed
    scale = np.abs(w).max() / qmax
    q = np.clip(np.round(w / scale), -qmax - 1, qmax).astype(np.int8)
    return q, np.float16(scale)

w = np.array([0.10, -0.42, 0.31, 0.07], dtype=np.float32)
q, s = quant_group(w)
w_hat = q.astype(np.float32) * np.float32(s)
print(q, float(s), w_hat)   # [ 2 -7  5  1] 0.06 [ 0.12 -0.42  0.3  0.06]

Kotlin, same idea:

import kotlin.math.abs
import kotlin.math.roundToInt

fun quantGroup(w: FloatArray, bits: Int = 4): Pair<IntArray, Float> {
    val qmax = (1 shl (bits - 1)) - 1                 // 7
    val scale = w.maxOf { abs(it) } / qmax
    val q = IntArray(w.size) { (w[it] / scale).roundToInt().coerceIn(-qmax - 1, qmax) }
    return q to scale
}

fun main() {
    val w = floatArrayOf(0.10f, -0.42f, 0.31f, 0.07f)
    val (q, s) = quantGroup(w)
    val back = FloatArray(w.size) { q[it] * s }
    println("${q.toList()} $s ${back.toList()}")      // [2, -7, 5, 1] 0.06 [0.12, -0.42, 0.3, 0.06]
}

Java, same idea:

import java.util.Arrays;

public class QuantDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        float[] w = {0.10f, -0.42f, 0.31f, 0.07f};
        int qmax = 7;
        float max = 0;
        for (float x : w) max = Math.max(max, Math.abs(x));
        float scale = max / qmax;
        int[] q = new int[w.length];
        float[] back = new float[w.length];
        for (int i = 0; i < w.length; i++) {
            q[i] = Math.max(-8, Math.min(7, Math.round(w[i] / scale)));
            back[i] = q[i] * scale;
        }
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(q) + " " + scale + " " + Arrays.toString(back));
        // [2, -7, 5, 1] 0.06 [0.12, -0.42, 0.3, 0.06]
    }
}

Real-world note: the rounding above is called round-to-nearest (RTN). It is the baseline every method tries to beat. GPTQ and AWQ exist because RTN at 4 bits visibly hurts quality on larger models, while still being what simple "Q4_0" style formats do (llama.cpp's newer k-quants and importance-matrix variants improve on that).

Everyday analogy: rounding prices on a restaurant menu to the nearest 5 rupees. For one dish the error is tiny. If one item costs 5,000, a single rounding step for that range makes every cheap item round to 0, which is why you give each section of the menu its own rounding step (a group scale).

Common interview traps.

  • Computing model size with exactly 4 bits per weight and ignoring scale/zero-point overhead (about 4.15 to 4.5 effective bits).
  • Not being able to explain why smaller groups improve accuracy (outliers poison a shared scale) and why they cost more memory.
  • Confusing quantization error (an approximation per weight) with the model being "retrained": PTQ never changes the architecture, only how numbers are stored.

notes.title: GPTQ explained
notes.html:
What it is. GPTQ (from the 2022 paper "GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers" by Frantar et al.) is a post-training method: you take a finished model, run a small calibration set of text through it (commonly a few hundred samples, for example from C4 or WikiText), and it outputs a 4-bit (or 3/8-bit) model without any gradient-based retraining.

Why it exists. Plain round-to-nearest treats every weight independently. But weights in a layer work together: output = W x input. If you round one weight badly, you can compensate by nudging other, not-yet-quantized weights so the layer's output stays close to the original. GPTQ automates that compensation.

How it works, plain version.

  1. Take one layer at a time (a weight matrix W). Capture the real inputs X that reach it when the calibration text runs through the model.
  2. The goal is to minimise the output error || W X - W_hat X ||^2, not the weight error. This distinction matters: weights that multiply large inputs matter more.
  3. Compute a matrix H = 2 X X^T (the Hessian, a measure of how sensitive the output is to each weight; the "second-order information" you read about).
  4. Quantize the weights column by column. After rounding column j, spread its rounding error onto the remaining unquantized columns using the inverse Hessian, so later columns absorb the mistake.
  5. Process in blocks (the paper uses lazy batch updates) so the algorithm is fast on a GPU. The paper reports quantizing a 175B-parameter model in a few GPU-hours (verify exact figure).
  6. Save the packed 4-bit integers, per-group scales and zero-points, plus a config (bits, group_size, desc_act, sym).
fp16 layer W  --(calibration inputs X)--> Hessian H
                                           |
      quantize column 1 -> error e1 -> push e1 onto columns 2..n (using H^-1)
      quantize column 2 -> error e2 -> push onto 3..n
      ...
      => 4-bit W_hat with group scales, output stays close to W X

Knobs you will see in a GPTQ model card.

  • bits: 4 is the mainstream choice; 3 and 8 exist.
  • group_size: 128 is the common default; 64 or 32 are more accurate and larger; -1 means one scale per whole row (smallest, least accurate).
  • desc_act ("act order"): quantize columns in order of descending activation size. Better accuracy, but older kernels were slower with it (verify with your runtime).
  • damp_percent: small number added to the Hessian diagonal for numerical stability.

Tools. AutoGPTQ (now largely unmaintained; verify status), GPTQModel (a maintained successor), llm-compressor from the vLLM project (supports GPTQ, AWQ and FP8 recipes), and Hugging Face transformers with GPTQConfig for loading and quantizing. Inference kernels: Marlin and ExLlama variants for fast 4-bit GPU matmul (vLLM uses Marlin kernels for GPTQ/AWQ on supported GPUs).

Loading a prequantized GPTQ model in Python (needs a GPTQ backend installed; repo id is a placeholder, so substitute a real one):

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

repo = "someorg/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-GPTQ-4bit"   # placeholder repo id
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(repo)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(repo, device_map="auto")
# the quantization_config stored in config.json tells transformers which backend to use

ids = tok("Explain GPTQ in one sentence.", return_tensors="pt").to(model.device)
out = model.generate(**ids, max_new_tokens=40)
print(tok.decode(out[0], skip_special_tokens=True))   # a short generated sentence

Kotlin and Java: GPTQ quantization and GPU kernels are Python/CUDA territory with no sensible JVM-native loader. From the JVM you consume a GPTQ model by calling a server that loaded it (vLLM or TGI exposing an OpenAI-compatible endpoint). Kotlin:

import java.net.URI
import java.net.http.HttpClient
import java.net.http.HttpRequest
import java.net.http.HttpResponse

fun main() {
    val body = """{"model":"someorg/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-GPTQ-4bit",
      "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Explain GPTQ in one sentence."}],"max_tokens":60}"""
    val req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI("http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions"))
        .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build()
    val res = HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString())
    println(res.body())   // JSON with choices[0].message.content
}

Java:

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.*;

public class CallGptqServer {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String body = "{\"model\":\"someorg/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-GPTQ-4bit\","
            + "\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"Explain GPTQ in one sentence.\"}],\"max_tokens\":60}";
        HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions"))
            .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
            .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build();
        System.out.println(HttpClient.newHttpClient()
            .send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body()); // JSON response
    }
}

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: a team of ten people splitting a restaurant bill and rounding each share to whole rupees. A naive approach rounds each share on its own. GPTQ is like the last person adjusting their share to absorb whatever the others rounded, so the total still matches.

Production failure patterns: (1) calibration data far from production traffic (English Wikipedia calibration, but you serve code or Hindi), so quality drops on your real domain; (2) a repo quantized with desc_act=True that your chosen kernel does not support, giving errors or slow throughput; (3) mixing quantization config and tokenizer versions between repos.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying GPTQ "retrains" the model. It does not; it is a one-shot, layer-wise, calibration-based post-training method.
  • Not knowing it minimises layer OUTPUT error using second-order (Hessian) information rather than raw weight error.
  • Forgetting calibration data matters: quantization quality is partly a function of how representative the calibration text is.
  • Assuming GPTQ always makes inference faster. It cuts memory reliably; speed depends on kernels (Marlin/ExLlama) and batch size.

notes.title: AWQ explained
notes.html:
What it is. AWQ, Activation-aware Weight Quantization (paper by Lin et al., MIT Han Lab, 2023; won a MLSys 2024 best paper award, verify), is another 4-bit weight-only post-training method with the same practical goal as GPTQ but a different insight.

The insight. Not all weights are equally important. A tiny fraction (the paper's headline observation is around 1 percent) of weight channels matter far more, and you find them by looking at the activations, not the weights: a channel that multiplies consistently large input activations contributes a lot to the output, so its rounding error is amplified. Protecting these "salient" channels recovers most of the lost accuracy.

How it avoids the obvious trap. The obvious fix is to keep salient channels in fp16 and quantize the rest, but mixed-precision storage is awkward and slow on hardware. AWQ gets the same effect with a mathematical trick:

  1. Run calibration data; record the average activation magnitude per input channel.
  2. For each salient channel, scale the weight up by a factor s before quantization. A bigger weight uses more of the integer range, so relative rounding error shrinks.
  3. Divide the matching activation by s (fused into the previous operation), so the mathematical product is unchanged.
  4. Pick s per channel by a small grid search (roughly s = activation_magnitude ^ alpha, searching alpha between 0 and 1) minimising output error.
  5. Quantize everything uniformly to 4 bits with group scales. All weights are the same type, so kernels stay simple and fast.
Before:  y = (w * s_free) x          rounding error hits important channel hard
AWQ:     y = (w * s) (x / s)         w*s uses larger integer range -> smaller relative error
         x/s is folded into the previous layer or norm, costs nothing at runtime

Worked mini example. Channel weight w = 0.06 in a group whose scale is 0.06 (from the earlier example): q = round(0.06/0.06) = 1, no error, but a nearby 0.07 rounded to 1 (0.06) has error 0.01 = 14 percent relative. If that channel is salient and we scale by s = 2: w*s = 0.14; the group max is still 0.42 (so scale stays 0.06 only if 0.14 does not change the max): q = round(0.14/0.06) = round(2.33) = 2 giving 0.12; divide by 2 at the end: 0.06. Error 0.01 again here because the example is tiny, but the key is the mechanism: larger value in the integer grid means a smaller relative error after division. In practice the gain appears across many weights in large layers, not in a 4-element toy. Treat this arithmetic as an illustration of the mechanism, not a benchmark.

GPTQ vs AWQ, honestly.

                    GPTQ                          AWQ
Core idea           compensate rounding errors     protect salient channels via scaling
                    with Hessian updates
Calibration need    needs more, can overfit it     fewer samples, less overfit risk
Quantization time   longer (per-layer solving)     faster (grid search of scales)
Quality at 4-bit    good                           often equal or slightly better, esp. on
                                                   instruction-tuned models (verify per model)
Serving             vLLM, TGI, transformers        vLLM, TGI, transformers, TensorRT-LLM

Treat any claimed winner as model-specific and verify with your own eval.

Python, quantizing with AutoAWQ (package name autoawq; its maintenance status has changed over time and llm-compressor is the actively developed alternative, so verify before adopting):

from awq import AutoAWQForCausalLM
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

src, dst = "meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct", "llama31-8b-awq"
model = AutoAWQForCausalLM.from_pretrained(src)
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(src)
cfg = {"zero_point": True, "q_group_size": 128, "w_bit": 4, "version": "GEMM"}
model.quantize(tok, quant_config=cfg)      # runs calibration (default dataset), finds scales
model.save_quantized(dst); tok.save_pretrained(dst)
print("saved", dst)   # a folder of safetensors, roughly a quarter to a third the fp16 size

Serving the result with vLLM (Python), where vLLM auto-detects the quantization from the checkpoint config:

from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

llm = LLM(model="llama31-8b-awq", quantization="awq")   # quantization arg optional if config present
out = llm.generate(["What is AWQ?"], SamplingParams(max_tokens=50))
print(out[0].outputs[0].text)   # generated text

Kotlin and Java: no JVM quantizer exists for AWQ. Calling an AWQ model uses the same OpenAI-compatible HTTP call shown in the GPTQ section; only the model field changes. One line is enough in Kotlin and Java: reuse that client with the model set to your AWQ repo name. Alternatively LangChain4j's OpenAI integration can be pointed at the server with a custom baseUrl (verify exact builder names in the LangChain4j docs).

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: packing a suitcase for a long flight with a weight limit. Instead of shrinking everything equally, you notice the 5 items you will use daily (salient channels) and pack those carefully in sturdy cases, while compressing the rarely used stuff harder.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing AWQ as "keeps 1 percent of weights in fp16". The point of the paper is that it does NOT do mixed precision; it rescales salient channels so everything stays uniform 4-bit.
  • Saying salient weights are found by weight magnitude. AWQ uses activation statistics.
  • Claiming AWQ "needs no data". It needs a small calibration set; it is just less sensitive to its content.
  • Declaring AWQ strictly better than GPTQ. Results vary by model; always run a task-specific eval.

notes.title: GGUF and the llama.cpp quant types
notes.html:
What it is. GGUF (GPT-Generated Unified Format) is the single-file model format used by llama.cpp and everything built on it. It replaced the older GGML/GGJT formats in 2023. One .gguf file contains: a header, key-value metadata (architecture, context length, number of layers and KV heads, tokenizer vocabulary and merges, chat template, rope settings), and the tensors (weights) in whatever quant types the creator chose. Because the tokenizer and architecture travel inside the file, you can run llama-cli -m model.gguf with nothing else.

Why it exists. Runtimes for laptops, phones and CPUs want: one file, memory-mappable (mmap, so the OS loads pages lazily and shares them across processes), extensible metadata without breaking old readers, and quantization types that give good speed on CPU SIMD (AVX2, ARM NEON) as well as Apple Metal, CUDA and Vulkan.

Block-based quantization. Weights are quantized in small blocks, each with its own scale.

Q4_0 block: 32 weights
  scale (fp16)             2 bytes
  32 x 4-bit values       16 bytes
  total                   18 bytes / 32 weights = 4.5 bits per weight

Q8_0 block: 32 weights
  scale (fp16)             2 bytes
  32 x int8               32 bytes
  total                   34 bytes / 32 = 8.5 bits per weight

K-quants. Names like Q4_K_M, Q5_K_S, Q6_K, Q3_K_L are k-quants. They use larger "super-blocks" (256 weights) made of smaller sub-blocks (for example 8 sub-blocks of 32) with their own quantized scales and minimums, giving better accuracy for the same bits. The suffix is the mix: S small, M medium, L large. In an _M file some sensitive tensors (for instance parts of attention v projections and the FFN down projection in some layers) use a higher-precision type than the rest, so a "Q4_K_M" file is a mixture and its real average is about 4.8 bits per weight (verify; it varies by model).

Rough size table (approximate bits per weight as commonly quoted by llama.cpp; verify with your actual file):

Type      ~bits/weight   7B file    70B file    Quality
Q2_K      ~2.6           ~2.7 GB    ~27 GB      noticeable loss
Q3_K_M    ~3.9           ~3.3 GB    ~34 GB      usable, lossy
Q4_K_M    ~4.8           ~4.1 GB    ~42 GB      sweet spot for most
Q5_K_M    ~5.7           ~4.8 GB    ~50 GB      near fp16 for most tasks
Q6_K      ~6.6           ~5.5 GB    ~58 GB      very close to fp16
Q8_0      ~8.5           ~7.2 GB    ~74 GB      practically lossless
F16       16             ~13.5 GB   ~140 GB     reference

Math check: a 7B model at 4.8 bits is 7e9 x 4.8 / 8 = 4.2e9 bytes, about 4.2 GB, matching the table. A 70B at 4.8 bits is 70e9 x 0.6 = 42 GB.

I-quants and imatrix. Types named IQ4_XS, IQ3_XXS, IQ2_M use codebook-style tricks to stay usable at 2 to 3 bits. They benefit strongly from an importance matrix (imatrix): you run calibration text through the model once, record how much each weight contributes, and then the quantizer spends precision where it matters. This is conceptually the same insight as AWQ and GPTQ (calibration data identifies sensitivity), applied inside llama.cpp's tooling (llama-imatrix, then llama-quantize --imatrix).

Making your own GGUF. Convert the Hugging Face model, then quantize:

python convert_hf_to_gguf.py ./Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --outtype f16 --outfile llama31-8b-f16.gguf
llama-quantize llama31-8b-f16.gguf llama31-8b-Q4_K_M.gguf Q4_K_M

Python, running the file with llama-cpp-python (a binding over llama.cpp):

from llama_cpp import Llama

llm = Llama(model_path="llama31-8b-Q4_K_M.gguf", n_ctx=4096, n_gpu_layers=-1)  # -1 = offload all layers if GPU build
res = llm.create_chat_completion(messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hi in 5 words."}], max_tokens=20)
print(res["choices"][0]["message"]["content"])   # a short greeting

Kotlin (Android): the realistic path is a llama.cpp build for ARM exposed through JNI. llama.cpp ships an Android example in its repository (examples/llama.android; verify current layout), and third-party wrappers exist. Typical on-device shape, with LlamaBridge standing in for such a JNI wrapper (not a real library name):

class ChatViewModel(private val llm: LlamaBridge) : ViewModel() {   // LlamaBridge = your JNI wrapper, hypothetical name
    suspend fun ask(prompt: String): String = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {
        llm.loadModel(File(filesDir, "qwen2.5-1.5b-q4_k_m.gguf").path)  // mmap-loaded GGUF, ~1 GB
        llm.generate(prompt, maxTokens = 128)                          // tokens decoded on the CPU
    }
}

Java (server side): for a JVM backend, either call a llama-server over HTTP (shown in the next section) or use a JNI binding such as java-llama.cpp (verify its current API and maintenance before relying on it). Plain HTTP is the stable choice, so there is no separate snippet here.

Real products: Ollama (pulls GGUF files, runs llama.cpp as its engine; the Modelfile FROM can point to a GGUF), LM Studio and GPT4All (desktop apps on GGUF), Jan, and many Android/iOS local-LLM apps. Google's on-device Gemini Nano uses a different stack (AI Edge / ML Kit GenAI), not GGUF.

Production failure patterns: (1) downloading Q4_0 thinking it equals Q4_K_M (older, lower quality at the same size); (2) a model's chat template inside the GGUF metadata differing from what the app sends, giving garbled or looping output; (3) mmap of a 40 GB file on a machine with 32 GB RAM, so the OS pages the weights in and out (disk thrash, very slow tokens per second); (4) context set larger than the metadata supports.

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: GGUF is like a self-contained travel kit: the suitcase (weights), the phrasebook (tokenizer) and the itinerary (architecture metadata) in one bag. K-quant types are how thoroughly you vacuum-seal different items: delicate things get less compression.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling GGUF "a quantization algorithm". It is a file format that holds tensors of several quant types.
  • Mixing up Q4_0 (simple blocks, 4.5 bits) with Q4_K_M (super-blocks plus a mix of types, about 4.8 bits average and noticeably better quality).
  • Not knowing that GGUF carries the tokenizer and chat template, a common source of "model replies with garbage" bugs.
  • Assuming GGUF is CPU-only. llama.cpp offloads layers to CUDA, Metal and Vulkan GPUs, and splits a model between GPU and CPU RAM.

notes.title: Choosing a format and running it
notes.html:
You now have the three families. The decision is usually short:

Where does it run?
  Datacenter NVIDIA GPU, many users  -> FP8 (H100/L40S/B200) or AWQ/GPTQ 4-bit, served by vLLM / TGI / TensorRT-LLM
  Laptop, Mac, CPU box, edge device  -> GGUF Q4_K_M (or Q5_K_M / Q8_0 if memory allows) via llama.cpp / Ollama
  Android / iOS app                  -> small model (1B to 4B) in GGUF, or Google AI Edge / MediaPipe LLM format
  Fine-tune on one GPU               -> QLoRA on a 4-bit NF4 base (bitsandbytes), not GPTQ/AWQ

Rules of thumb that hold up:

  • Memory first. Pick the largest model whose quantized weights plus KV cache fit your GPU. A bigger model at 4-bit generally beats a smaller model at 16-bit at the same memory (the empirical finding behind much of the "run 4-bit" advice; still verify on your task).
  • Do not go below 4 bits for important work unless you evaluated it. Q3 and Q2 types degrade reasoning and code noticeably, especially for models under about 13B.
  • Check kernel support. A 4-bit checkpoint is only fast if your GPU architecture has a good kernel for it (Marlin needs Ampere or newer for the fast GPTQ/AWQ path; verify per vLLM version).
  • At large batch sizes, weight-only 4-bit gains shrink. Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound at small batch (so fewer bytes per weight means faster tokens), but at big batches the GPU becomes compute-bound and dequantization overhead eats the gain. That is why high-throughput H100 serving prefers FP8 (real FP8 tensor-core math).

Quick speed estimate for decode, to show the logic. Each generated token must read all weights from GPU memory once (single stream). For a 70B model at 4-bit (about 40 GB) on a GPU with about 2 TB/s bandwidth (an A100 80GB is about 2.0 TB/s; verify spec of your card):

tokens/s upper bound = bandwidth / bytes_read_per_token
                     = 2,000 GB/s / 40 GB = 50 tokens/s   (single stream, ideal)
fp16 would be 140 GB -> 2,000/140 = 14 tokens/s, but does not fit one GPU anyway

Real systems reach a fraction of this bound (often 50 to 80 percent for a well-tuned stack). Batching raises total throughput because the weights are read once for many sequences.

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: choosing a vehicle. FP8 on a datacenter GPU is a freight train (best at volume), AWQ/GPTQ is a delivery van (compact, versatile), GGUF is a bicycle that goes everywhere including a staircase (your phone) but does not carry as much.

Common interview traps.

  • Recommending GPTQ or AWQ for CPU-only or Apple Silicon deployment. That is GGUF territory.
  • Quoting a speedup from quantization without specifying batch size. The gain is largest at batch 1 and shrinks as you become compute-bound.
  • Choosing 2-bit or 3-bit to "make it fit" without an eval on the real task.
  • Forgetting the KV cache when checking whether a quantized model fits (covered in the memory sections below).

notes.title: TGI, Hugging Face Text Generation Inference
notes.html:
What it is. TGI (Text Generation Inference) is Hugging Face's production inference server for LLMs, written mostly in Rust (router, scheduling) with Python and CUDA kernels for the model. It exposes an HTTP API (including an OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions route) and a native /generate and /generate_stream API. Hugging Face used it to power their Inference Endpoints and the Hugging Face Chat product.

Status note, verify. As of recent announcements Hugging Face has said TGI is in maintenance mode and recommends engines such as vLLM or SGLang for new deployments. Check the TGI repository README for the current position before choosing it for a greenfield project. It still matters for interviews because many existing systems run it and its concepts are shared with vLLM.

What it provides.

  • Continuous batching: new requests join the running batch at each decode step instead of waiting for a full batch to finish (see C2/notes/01_I1.md for the mechanism).
  • Token streaming via Server-Sent Events.
  • Paged / flash attention kernels and tensor parallelism (--num-shard) to split one model across several GPUs.
  • Quantization options: --quantize accepts values such as bitsandbytes, bitsandbytes-nf4, gptq, awq, eetq, fp8 (verify the current list in text-generation-launcher --help).
  • Prefix caching, speculative decoding, structured output ("grammar"/JSON guidance), watermarking and safetensors loading.
  • Prometheus metrics and OpenTelemetry tracing for production monitoring.

Running it (Docker; image tag is a placeholder, check the registry for the current tag):

docker run --gpus all --shm-size 1g -p 8080:80 \
  -v $PWD/data:/data -e HF_TOKEN=$HF_TOKEN \
  ghcr.io/huggingface/text-generation-inference:<version> \
  --model-id someorg/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-AWQ \
  --quantize awq \
  --max-input-tokens 4096 --max-total-tokens 6144 \
  --max-batch-prefill-tokens 8192

The three length flags are the ones that bite in production. max-input-tokens is the longest prompt, max-total-tokens is prompt plus generated tokens per request, and max-batch-prefill-tokens caps tokens processed in one prefill step (it controls the memory spike during prompt processing). Set them from your real traffic, because TGI pre-computes how much KV cache the GPU can hold and rejects requests that exceed limits.

Python client with huggingface_hub (use InferenceClient, which can point at any TGI or compatible URL):

from huggingface_hub import InferenceClient

client = InferenceClient("http://localhost:8080")
for chunk in client.chat_completion(
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Why is the sky blue? One line."}],
        max_tokens=60, stream=True):
    print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content or "", end="")   # tokens arrive as they are generated

Kotlin, streaming the OpenAI-compatible route with the JDK HttpClient (lines starting with data: are SSE events):

import java.net.URI
import java.net.http.*

fun main() {
    val body = """{"model":"tgi","stream":true,"max_tokens":60,
      "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Why is the sky blue? One line."}]}"""
    val req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI("http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions"))
        .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build()
    HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofLines()).body()
        .filter { it.startsWith("data:") }.forEach(::println)   // one JSON chunk per line, ends with data: [DONE]
}

Java:

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.*;

public class TgiStream {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String body = "{\"model\":\"tgi\",\"stream\":true,\"max_tokens\":60,"
            + "\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"Why is the sky blue? One line.\"}]}";
        HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions"))
            .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
            .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build();
        HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofLines()).body()
            .filter(l -> l.startsWith("data:")).forEach(System.out::println);
    }
}

Production failure patterns: (1) startup OOM because max-total-tokens x expected batch exceeds the cache the GPU can hold (TGI logs how many tokens of KV cache it allocated, so read that line); (2) 4xx errors on long prompts because max-input-tokens was left at default; (3) cold start of minutes when a 40 GB model is downloaded at pod start rather than baked into the image or a persistent volume; (4) forgetting --shm-size which breaks multi-GPU communication.

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: TGI is a restaurant kitchen with a smart expediter. Orders (requests) arrive any time, the expediter lets new orders join the pans already on the stove (continuous batching), and sends out each dish the moment it is ready rather than waiting for the whole table (streaming).

Common interview traps.

  • Describing TGI as a model. It is a serving engine; the model is whatever --model-id points to.
  • Not mentioning that TGI, vLLM and SGLang overlap heavily (continuous batching, paged KV cache), so the real selection criteria are kernel support, feature set, community health and your GPU.
  • Setting limits arbitrarily. Over-large max-total-tokens shrinks effective concurrency; too small rejects legitimate requests.
  • Forgetting that Hugging Face has signalled maintenance mode (verify) when asked what you would pick for a new project.

notes.title: llama.cpp and its server
notes.html:
What it is. llama.cpp (by Georgi Gerganov, started March 2023) is a C/C++ inference engine for LLMs with no heavy dependencies. It is built on ggml, a small tensor library. It runs GGUF models on CPU first, and also on Apple Metal, NVIDIA CUDA, AMD HIP/ROCm, Vulkan, SYCL and others. It is the engine behind Ollama and many desktop apps.

Why it matters. It brought LLMs to ordinary hardware: a 7B Q4_K_M model (about 4 GB) runs on a laptop with 8 GB RAM, at some tokens per second on CPU and far faster on Apple Silicon (whose unified memory has high bandwidth, for example about 100 GB/s on base M-series chips up to 400 to 800 GB/s on Max/Ultra; verify per chip).

Tools that ship with it.

  • llama-cli: chat or one-shot completion in the terminal.
  • llama-server: an HTTP server with an OpenAI-compatible API (/v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions, /v1/embeddings), a built-in web UI, and Prometheus metrics (flag-enabled). It supports parallel slots, continuous batching, prompt caching, grammar-constrained (JSON) output, speculative decoding and multimodal models in recent versions (verify per version).
  • llama-bench: measures prompt processing (pp) and token generation (tg) speed.
  • llama-quantize, llama-imatrix: the quantization toolchain from the GGUF section.

Key runtime flags (names have been stable but check --help of your build):

llama-server -m llama31-8b-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  -c 16384          # total context shared by all slots
  -np 4             # 4 parallel slots -> each slot gets 16384/4 = 4096 tokens
  -ngl 99           # offload up to 99 layers to the GPU (all of them for a small model)
  -t 8              # CPU threads for the part running on CPU
  --port 8081

Important detail that catches people: -c (context size) is the total KV cache across slots, split by -np. With -c 16384 -np 4 each request can use only 4,096 tokens of context. Teams wonder why long prompts are truncated under concurrency; this is the reason.

GPU/CPU split. -ngl N puts N transformer layers on the GPU and keeps the rest in system RAM. Example: a 70B Q4_K_M (about 42 GB) with a 24 GB GPU can hold roughly half the layers; speed lands between pure-CPU and pure-GPU because every token still passes through the CPU-side layers (and the slowest part sets the pace).

Python, calling llama-server using the OpenAI SDK pointed at it:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8081/v1", api_key="not-needed")   # llama-server ignores the key by default
r = client.chat.completions.create(model="local", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Name 3 fruits."}], max_tokens=30)
print(r.choices[0].message.content)   # e.g. "Apple, banana, mango."

Kotlin (the JVM-side client, reusing the JDK HttpClient; on Android the same request goes to your own backend, not directly to a phone-side secret):

import java.net.URI
import java.net.http.*

fun main() {
    val body = """{"model":"local","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Name 3 fruits."}],"max_tokens":30}"""
    val req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI("http://localhost:8081/v1/chat/completions"))
        .header("Content-Type", "application/json").POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build()
    println(HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body())  // OpenAI-shaped JSON
}

Java:

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.*;

public class LlamaServerCall {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String body = "{\"model\":\"local\",\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"Name 3 fruits.\"}],\"max_tokens\":30}";
        HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("http://localhost:8081/v1/chat/completions"))
            .header("Content-Type", "application/json").POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build();
        System.out.println(HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body());
    }
}

Where llama.cpp is NOT the best choice: a multi-user, high-throughput GPU service. vLLM, TGI, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM have better batching, scheduling and multi-GPU support for that workload. llama.cpp shines for local, single-user or small-team, edge, mixed CPU/GPU, and cases where you need a tiny deployable binary.

Production failure patterns: (1) swapping because the model plus KV cache exceed RAM (check with llama-bench and watch for tokens/s collapsing); (2) concurrency surprises from the -c / -np split; (3) CPU thread oversubscription (-t larger than physical cores slows decoding); (4) running a CPU-only build on a GPU machine and wondering why it is slow (confirm the backend in the startup log).

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: llama.cpp is a pocket multi-tool: it fits anywhere and does the job on a campsite, but you would not use it to run a factory floor.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing llama.cpp is "just for hobbyists". It is a serious engine used inside Ollama, LM Studio and many commercial local-AI features, although it is not the throughput leader on datacenter GPUs.
  • Misreading -c with parallel slots (context per request is c / np).
  • Quoting CPU speed without noting memory bandwidth is the limit, not core count. Decode speed is about bandwidth divided by model bytes, as in the previous section.
  • Forgetting that -ngl partial offload makes the slow side (CPU) dominate.

notes.title: Triton Inference Server
notes.html:
What it is. NVIDIA Triton Inference Server (now branded in NVIDIA docs as part of the Dynamo/Triton line; verify current naming) is a general-purpose, production model-serving system. It is not LLM-specific: it serves TensorFlow, PyTorch, ONNX, TensorRT, OpenVINO, Python-code and other models through pluggable backends. For LLMs, it hosts the TensorRT-LLM backend (NVIDIA's optimized LLM engine) or the vLLM backend.

Do not confuse it with OpenAI Triton, the Python-like language for writing GPU kernels (used inside PyTorch's torch.compile and vLLM kernels). Same word, unrelated projects. Interviewers like this trap.

Why teams use it.

  • One server for many model types: a recommender, an embedding model, a reranker, an image model and an LLM, behind one consistent API and one metrics stack.
  • Model repository: a directory (local, S3, GCS) with one folder per model, version subfolders and a config.pbtxt. Triton loads, unloads and hot-reloads models from it.
  • Dynamic batching: collects individual requests for a few microseconds up to a configured delay and runs them as one batch.
  • Concurrent model execution: several model instances on one GPU (instance_group), or across GPUs.
  • Ensembles and BLS (business logic scripting): chain tokenizer -> model -> detokenizer as a pipeline inside the server.
  • Protocols: HTTP/REST and gRPC following the KServe v2 inference protocol, plus a C API; Prometheus metrics endpoint; model analyzer for tuning.

Repository layout:

model_repository/
  llama31_8b/
    config.pbtxt            # backend, max_batch_size, inputs/outputs, instance_group, dynamic_batching
    1/                      # version 1
      model.py  or  engine files

A tiny config.pbtxt shape for a Python-backend model (illustrative; LLM configs for TensorRT-LLM have many more fields, so copy NVIDIA's template for those):

name: "embedder"
backend: "python"
max_batch_size: 16
input  [ { name: "TEXT"  data_type: TYPE_STRING dims: [1] } ]
output [ { name: "EMBED" data_type: TYPE_FP32   dims: [384] } ]
instance_group [ { kind: KIND_GPU count: 1 } ]
dynamic_batching { max_queue_delay_microseconds: 5000 }

How it handles an LLM request with TensorRT-LLM (conceptually): the request enters Triton, the TensorRT-LLM backend uses in-flight batching (NVIDIA's term for continuous batching) and a paged KV cache, and tokens are returned by streaming in decoupled mode. TensorRT-LLM needs a compile step: you build an optimized engine for a specific model, GPU architecture, precision (fp16, FP8, INT4 AWQ, INT4 GPTQ), max batch and max sequence length. That brings top speed on NVIDIA GPUs, and costs flexibility (rebuild when anything changes, engine tied to GPU type).

Python client with tritonclient (HTTP; the model name and tensor names must match your config.pbtxt):

import numpy as np
import tritonclient.http as httpclient

client = httpclient.InferenceServerClient(url="localhost:8000")
inp = httpclient.InferInput("TEXT", [1, 1], "BYTES")
inp.set_data_from_numpy(np.array([["hello world"]], dtype=object))
res = client.infer("embedder", inputs=[inp])
print(res.as_numpy("EMBED").shape)   # (1, 384)

Kotlin, the same call over the KServe v2 REST protocol (no Triton client library needed; POST /v2/models/<name>/infer):

import java.net.URI
import java.net.http.*

fun main() {
    val body = """{"inputs":[{"name":"TEXT","shape":[1,1],"datatype":"BYTES","data":["hello world"]}]}"""
    val req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI("http://localhost:8000/v2/models/embedder/infer"))
        .header("Content-Type", "application/json").POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build()
    println(HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body())  // JSON with outputs[0].data (384 floats)
}

Java (gRPC is the other option for high-volume traffic: generate stubs from Triton's grpc_service.proto):

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.*;

public class TritonInfer {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String body = "{\"inputs\":[{\"name\":\"TEXT\",\"shape\":[1,1],\"datatype\":\"BYTES\",\"data\":[\"hello world\"]}]}";
        HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("http://localhost:8000/v2/models/embedder/infer"))
            .header("Content-Type", "application/json").POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build();
        System.out.println(HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body());
    }
}

Useful health endpoints: GET /v2/health/ready, GET /v2/models/<name>/ready, and metrics on port 8002 by default (verify for your deployment). Those map directly onto Kubernetes readiness probes and Prometheus scraping.

Real users: NVIDIA's own reference stacks, cloud managed services that expose Triton (for example Amazon SageMaker's Triton containers and Google Vertex AI custom containers; verify the current offering), and companies that serve mixed model fleets (recommendation plus search plus LLM) from a single platform.

Production failure patterns: (1) config mismatches (wrong tensor name or dims) give 400 errors that look like model bugs; (2) TensorRT-LLM engine built for H100 is loaded on A100, which fails (engines are GPU-architecture-specific); (3) dynamic batching delay set too high, adding latency to every request; (4) model repository on slow network storage, giving slow cold starts and slow hot reloads.

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: Triton is an airport ground-handling company. It does not care whether the aircraft is a small turboprop or a jumbo jet (model types); it provides gates, fuel, baggage belts and a schedule (model repository, batching, metrics). A specialist team (TensorRT-LLM) is brought in for the biggest planes (LLMs).

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing NVIDIA Triton Inference Server with OpenAI Triton (the kernel language).
  • Calling Triton an LLM server only. It is a general serving platform; LLM serving is one backend.
  • Ignoring that TensorRT-LLM engines are compiled per GPU architecture and per max shape.
  • Using Triton for a single small LLM when vLLM alone would be simpler. Choose Triton for heterogeneous fleets and NVIDIA-tuned stacks, not by default.

notes.title: Picking a serving framework
notes.html:
Now compare the engines you can name. Keep this table as an interview cheat sheet (features move quickly, so verify against current docs):

Engine            Strong at                          Formats / quant                 Watch out for
----------------  ---------------------------------  ------------------------------  ---------------------------------
vLLM              high-throughput GPU serving,       HF safetensors, GPTQ, AWQ, FP8,  needs NVIDIA/AMD/TPU stack;
                  PagedAttention, wide model support GGUF (experimental, verify)      memory tuning via gpu-memory-utilization
TGI               HF ecosystem, simple Docker        safetensors, GPTQ, AWQ, bnb, FP8 maintenance mode (verify)
SGLang            structured generation, prefix      safetensors, AWQ, GPTQ, FP8      newer, fast-moving
                  reuse (RadixAttention)
TensorRT-LLM      peak NVIDIA performance            FP8, INT4 AWQ/GPTQ, INT8         engine build step, GPU-specific
(via Triton)
llama.cpp         CPU / Apple / edge / mixed         GGUF                             weaker at big multi-user batching
Ollama            easiest local dev experience       GGUF (via llama.cpp)             not a high-scale server

Decision heuristics:

  1. Prototype on a laptop: Ollama or llama-server with a GGUF.
  2. Production on NVIDIA GPUs, one model family, many users: vLLM first (largest community), TensorRT-LLM via Triton if you need the last 20 to 40 percent and can afford the build step and NVIDIA lock-in (the gain varies a lot; benchmark it yourself).
  3. A fleet of different model types (ranker, embedder, LLM) with one operations story: Triton.
  4. Edge, offline, or air-gapped: llama.cpp.
  5. Android/iOS: do not ship server-class engines; use a small GGUF via llama.cpp or Google's AI Edge / MediaPipe LLM Inference, and call your backend for large models.

Also keep an API-compatibility layer in your architecture: every engine above can expose an OpenAI-style endpoint, so your application code (and your Spring AI or LangChain4j configuration) targets one interface and the engine becomes a deployment detail. A minimal Kotlin sketch of that idea:

// Same client code for vLLM, TGI, llama-server, Ollama: only baseUrl and model change.
data class LlmEndpoint(val baseUrl: String, val model: String)

val endpoints = mapOf(
    "prod-gpu" to LlmEndpoint("http://vllm.internal:8000/v1", "someorg/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-AWQ"),
    "dev-laptop" to LlmEndpoint("http://localhost:11434/v1", "llama3.1:8b")   // Ollama's OpenAI-compatible route
)

Python version of the same routing idea:

from openai import OpenAI

ENDPOINTS = {
    "prod-gpu": ("http://vllm.internal:8000/v1", "someorg/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-AWQ"),
    "dev-laptop": ("http://localhost:11434/v1", "llama3.1:8b"),
}

def client_for(env: str):
    base, model = ENDPOINTS[env]
    return OpenAI(base_url=base, api_key="unused"), model   # a client plus the model name to pass

Java version:

import java.util.Map;

public class Endpoints {
    record LlmEndpoint(String baseUrl, String model) {}

    static final Map<String, LlmEndpoint> ENDPOINTS = Map.of(
        "prod-gpu", new LlmEndpoint("http://vllm.internal:8000/v1", "someorg/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-AWQ"),
        "dev-laptop", new LlmEndpoint("http://localhost:11434/v1", "llama3.1:8b"));
}

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: choosing a transport for goods: a scooter (Ollama) for local deliveries, a van (vLLM) for the city, a freight train (TensorRT-LLM via Triton) for the busiest corridor, with one standard shipping label (the OpenAI-compatible API) so the sender does not care which one carries the parcel.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "use the fastest one" without naming workload, hardware and ops constraints.
  • Picking an engine by a vendor benchmark without testing your own prompt/output length mix and concurrency.
  • Coupling application code to one engine's native API rather than an OpenAI-compatible layer.
  • Overlooking licensing and support (open-source community versus vendor-supported stacks).

notes.title: GPU memory math for model weights
notes.html:
This is the arithmetic that decides whether anything fits. Learn it as three buckets: weights + KV cache + overhead/activations. We start with weights.

Formula.

weight_bytes = parameters x bytes_per_weight

Use decimal GB (1 GB = 1e9 bytes) for quick estimates and remember GPUs are sold in GB while tools sometimes print GiB (1 GiB = 1.0737e9 bytes, about 7.4 percent more). An "80 GB" A100/H100 has 80 GiB of physical memory in some tooling (nvidia-smi shows MiB; an 80 GB card reports about 81,920 MiB, verify on your hardware), so leave a margin and do not trade GB and GiB loosely.

Examples:

 7B  fp16:  7e9  x 2    = 14 GB        8B  fp16: 16 GB
 8B  4-bit: 8e9  x 0.53 = 4.2 GB (using 4.25 bits incl. scales -> 0.531 bytes)
13B  fp16: 26 GB     13B 4-bit: 13e9 x 0.53 = 6.9 GB
70B  fp16: 140 GB    70B fp8: 70 GB    70B 4-bit: 70e9 x 0.53 = 37 GB
405B fp16: 810 GB    405B fp8: 405 GB  405B 4-bit: ~215 GB

Check on the 405B 4-bit: 405e9 x 4.25 / 8 = 215e9 bytes = about 215 GB; so it needs at least 3 x 80 GB, and in practice 4 or 8 GPUs once KV cache and tensor-parallel overhead are added.

Notes:

  • Parameter counts printed as "70B" are rounded. Llama 3.1 70B is about 70.6B parameters; always read the real count from the model card or model.num_parameters().
  • Embeddings and output head are large for big vocabularies and are often left in higher precision by quantizers. The "all 4-bit" estimate is therefore a slight underestimate (add a few percent).
  • Mixture-of-experts models (Mixtral 8x7B, DeepSeek-V3 and similar) must hold ALL experts in memory even though only a few are active per token. Mixtral 8x7B is about 46.7B total parameters (about 13B active per token), so its fp16 memory is about 93 GB, not 26 GB. Compute cost follows active parameters; memory follows total parameters.
  • Multi-GPU: with tensor parallelism across N GPUs each holds about 1/N of the weights (plus replicated pieces such as embeddings in some designs). Pipeline parallelism splits by layers.

Python, a reusable calculator for weight memory:

def weight_gb(params_billion: float, bits: float) -> float:
    """Memory for weights in decimal GB. bits includes scale overhead (e.g. 4.25 for 4-bit g128)."""
    return params_billion * 1e9 * bits / 8 / 1e9

for name, p, b in [("8B fp16", 8, 16), ("8B 4-bit", 8, 4.25), ("70B fp16", 70, 16), ("70B 4-bit", 70, 4.25)]:
    print(f"{name:10s} {weight_gb(p, b):7.1f} GB")
# 8B fp16 16.0, 8B 4-bit 4.2, 70B fp16 140.0, 70B 4-bit 37.2

Kotlin:

fun weightGb(paramsBillion: Double, bits: Double): Double = paramsBillion * bits / 8.0   // billions x bytes = GB

fun main() {
    listOf("8B fp16" to (8.0 to 16.0), "70B 4-bit" to (70.0 to 4.25)).forEach { (n, pb) ->
        println("%-10s %.1f GB".format(n, weightGb(pb.first, pb.second)))   // 16.0 GB and 37.2 GB
    }
}

Java:

public class WeightMem {
    static double weightGb(double paramsBillion, double bits) { return paramsBillion * bits / 8.0; }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.printf("8B fp16   %.1f GB%n", weightGb(8, 16));      // 16.0 GB
        System.out.printf("70B 4-bit %.1f GB%n", weightGb(70, 4.25));   // 37.2 GB
    }
}

Training memory is a different, much larger number. Full fine-tuning with Adam in mixed precision needs roughly 16 bytes per parameter (2 bytes fp16 weights + 2 bytes gradients + 4 bytes fp32 master weights + 8 bytes for the two Adam moments = 16, a commonly cited figure from the ZeRO paper; activations extra). A 7B model then needs about 7e9 x 16 = 112 GB before activations, which is why LoRA/QLoRA exist. Inference needs only the weights plus cache.

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: weights are the luggage you must carry no matter what: a fixed baseline. Quantization is vacuum-packing the clothes. Count the luggage first; then see what room remains for the passengers (KV cache).

Common interview traps.

  • Using "parameters x 2 bytes" for a quantized model, or "parameters x 0.5 bytes" for 4-bit and forgetting scale overhead.
  • Sizing MoE models by active parameters instead of total parameters.
  • Mixing GB and GiB and being short of memory at the end.
  • Quoting inference memory for a training question (training needs roughly 8x more per parameter with Adam, as derived above).

notes.title: KV cache math and the full memory budget
notes.html:
What the KV cache is, briefly. During generation each transformer layer stores, for every token already seen, a key vector and a value vector so it does not recompute them for each new token. That store is the KV cache. It grows with tokens and with the number of simultaneous requests, and for long contexts or many users it can exceed the weights. (See C2/notes/01_I1.md for PagedAttention, which manages this memory; here we do the arithmetic.)

Formula.

kv_bytes_per_token = 2 (K and V) x n_layers x n_kv_heads x head_dim x bytes_per_element
kv_total           = kv_bytes_per_token x tokens_in_flight
tokens_in_flight   = sum over active requests of (prompt tokens + generated tokens so far)

The important variable is n_kv_heads. Older models used multi-head attention (MHA), where kv heads equal query heads. Modern models use grouped-query attention (GQA), where several query heads share one K/V head, shrinking the cache a lot. Read it from config.json (num_key_value_heads).

Worked examples (fp16 cache = 2 bytes; the layer/head numbers are from the published configs of these models, verify against the model card):

Llama 2 7B (MHA): 32 layers, 32 kv heads, head_dim 128
  per token = 2 x 32 x 32 x 128 x 2 bytes = 524,288 B = 0.5 MiB
  4,096-token context -> 4,096 x 0.5 MiB = 2 GiB per request

Llama 3.1 8B (GQA): 32 layers, 8 kv heads, head_dim 128
  per token = 2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 131,072 B = 128 KiB
  8,192 tokens -> 1 GiB per request;  32 concurrent such requests -> 32 GiB

Llama 3.1 70B (GQA): 80 layers, 8 kv heads, head_dim 128
  per token = 2 x 80 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 327,680 B = 320 KiB (about 0.33 MB)
  8,192 tokens -> 2.5 GiB per request;  128,000 tokens -> 40 GiB for ONE request

Compare Llama 2 7B at 0.5 MiB per token with Llama 3.1 8B at 128 KiB per token: GQA cut the per-token cache by a factor of 4 (32 kv heads to 8). With fp8 KV cache the element size is 1 byte, halving all the above (vLLM option --kv-cache-dtype fp8; verify support on your GPU and test accuracy on long contexts).

Other buckets.

  • Activations / workspace: temporary tensors during the forward pass. In inference this is small for decode but can spike during prefill of long prompts (the reason for TGI's max-batch-prefill-tokens and vLLM's max-num-batched-tokens). Budget a few GB for 8B to 70B models; measure.
  • CUDA context and framework overhead: about 0.5 to 1.5 GB per GPU for the CUDA context, cuBLAS/cuDNN workspaces and the PyTorch allocator (verify in your stack).
  • Fragmentation: naive contiguous KV allocation wastes memory; PagedAttention reduces waste to a few percent (vLLM paper reports large reductions in waste; verify exact numbers there).
  • CUDA graphs and engine buffers in vLLM/TensorRT-LLM take extra memory at startup.
  • Tensor-parallel communication buffers when sharding over GPUs (NVLink all-reduce buffers).

vLLM's budgeting in one line. With --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90, vLLM may use 90 percent of each GPU's memory. It loads weights, profiles a forward pass to measure peak activation memory, and gives everything left to the KV cache pool. So:

KV pool = 0.90 x GPU_mem - weights - activation_peak - overhead

Full worked example: serve Llama 3.1 70B with 4-bit AWQ on one 80 GB GPU.

GPU memory                                   80.0 GB (treat as decimal for the estimate)
Usable at 0.90                               72.0 GB
Weights 4.25 bits: 70.6e9 x 4.25/8 =         37.5 GB
Activations + CUDA overhead (estimate)       ~4.0 GB
KV pool = 72.0 - 37.5 - 4.0 =                30.5 GB
Cache per token (fp16 KV) = 320 KiB = 0.328 MB   -> 30.5e9 / 327,680 = 93,078 tokens
Concurrent requests of 3,000 tokens (prompt+output): 93,078 / 3,000 = 31 requests
With fp8 KV cache: 186,000 tokens -> 62 requests

Python, a full budget estimator that mirrors the arithmetic above:

def kv_bytes_per_token(layers: int, kv_heads: int, head_dim: int, bytes_per_el: int = 2) -> int:
    return 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * bytes_per_el

def plan(gpu_gb, util, params_b, w_bits, layers, kv_heads, head_dim, overhead_gb, req_tokens, kv_bytes=2):
    weights = params_b * w_bits / 8                      # GB
    pool = gpu_gb * util - weights - overhead_gb         # GB left for KV cache
    per_tok = kv_bytes_per_token(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, kv_bytes)
    tokens = pool * 1e9 / per_tok
    return weights, pool, tokens, tokens / req_tokens

w, pool, toks, reqs = plan(80, 0.90, 70.6, 4.25, 80, 8, 128, 4.0, 3000)
print(f"weights {w:.1f} GB, kv pool {pool:.1f} GB, {toks:,.0f} tokens, {reqs:.0f} requests")
# weights 37.5 GB, kv pool 30.5 GB, 93,118 tokens, 31 requests

Kotlin:

fun kvBytesPerToken(layers: Int, kvHeads: Int, headDim: Int, bytesPerEl: Int = 2): Long =
    2L * layers * kvHeads * headDim * bytesPerEl

fun main() {
    val weights = 70.6 * 4.25 / 8                      // GB
    val pool = 80 * 0.90 - weights - 4.0               // GB for KV
    val perTok = kvBytesPerToken(80, 8, 128)           // 327,680 bytes
    val tokens = pool * 1e9 / perTok
    println("weights %.1f GB, pool %.1f GB, %.0f tokens, %.0f requests".format(weights, pool, tokens, tokens / 3000))
    // weights 37.5 GB, pool 30.5 GB, ~93,118 tokens, ~31 requests
}

Java:

public class GpuPlan {
    static long kvBytesPerToken(int layers, int kvHeads, int headDim, int bytesPerEl) {
        return 2L * layers * kvHeads * headDim * bytesPerEl;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double weights = 70.6 * 4.25 / 8;                    // GB
        double pool = 80 * 0.90 - weights - 4.0;             // GB left for KV cache
        long perTok = kvBytesPerToken(80, 8, 128, 2);        // 327,680 bytes
        double tokens = pool * 1e9 / perTok;
        System.out.printf("weights %.1f GB, pool %.1f GB, %.0f tokens, %.0f requests%n",
            weights, pool, tokens, tokens / 3000);
        // weights 37.5 GB, pool 30.5 GB, ~93,118 tokens, ~31 requests
    }
}

Interview habit: after the memory fit, check throughput, because fitting is necessary but not sufficient. A single 80 GB GPU running the 4-bit 70B above is bandwidth-bound at about 2,000 GB/s / 37.5 GB = 53 tokens/s per stream in the ideal single-stream case; batching 31 streams lifts aggregate output well above that, but each user sees tokens/s well below the single-stream ideal. Whether that meets your latency SLO is a benchmark question (see C2/notes/03_C1.md for the sizing process and cost side).

Production failure patterns:

  • OOM only under load: weights fit at startup, then bursts of long prompts exhaust the cache. Symptoms: CUDA out of memory in prefill, or vLLM preempting/recomputing requests (watch its preemption counter), latency spikes. Fix: lower max-model-len, cap concurrency, quantize KV cache, or add a GPU.
  • Long-context surprise: a feature allows 128k contexts; one such request alone takes 40 GiB of KV cache on the 70B above (computed earlier), starving everyone else. Fix: per-tenant limits and prompt-length caps.
  • Utilization set to 0.98 for "more cache": leaves no room for transient spikes and fragmentation of other processes (and other users of the same GPU), causing random OOM. Keep 0.85 to 0.92 unless you measured.
  • Wrong kv-head count in a spreadsheet: using the number of attention heads (64 for 70B) instead of kv heads (8) overestimates cache 8x and makes you buy GPUs you do not need.
  • Forgetting that parallel requests multiply the cache while the weights stay fixed.

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: a hotel. The building (weights) is fixed. Each guest (request) needs a room whose size grows the longer they stay and the more luggage they bring (tokens). Staff areas and lifts (overhead) take floor space too. The number of guests you can host is what is left after the building and staff areas are subtracted.

Common interview traps.

  • Using attention heads instead of KV heads in the formula (the GQA mistake) and being off by 4x to 8x.
  • Forgetting the factor of 2 for keys AND values.
  • Computing cache for one request only; the cache scales with concurrent tokens.
  • Ignoring activation and overhead memory, or setting GPU utilization so high that spikes crash the server.
  • Assuming that a model that "loads" will serve production traffic; loading proves only the weights fit.

notes.title: Debugging out-of-memory and tuning checklist
notes.html:
A short, practical checklist you can recite in an interview or use at 2 a.m.

Symptoms and first suspects.

Symptom                                   First suspect
----------------------------------------  --------------------------------------------------
OOM at startup, weights loading           weights + overhead > GPU; need quantization or more GPUs
Starts fine, OOM after minutes of traffic KV cache full / long prompts / too many concurrent seqs
OOM only on certain prompts               prefill activation spike; reduce max batched tokens
Slow tokens/s with free GPU memory        CPU offload (-ngl too low), swapping, or compute-bound dequant
Garbage text after quantizing             bad calibration, wrong chat template, or too-low bits
Throughput lower than expected            batch too small, kernel not optimized for this GPU/quant

Levers, cheapest first.

  1. Lower max-model-len / max-total-tokens to what your product truly needs.
  2. Cap concurrency (max-num-seqs in vLLM, slots in llama.cpp).
  3. Quantize the KV cache to fp8 or int8 and evaluate long-context quality.
  4. Move from 16-bit to FP8 or 4-bit weights.
  5. Shard over more GPUs with tensor parallelism (cost: interconnect and communication overhead).
  6. Reduce unneeded features: speculative decoding draft models and large CUDA-graph capture sets use memory.
  7. Last, buy more or bigger GPUs.

Validate every change with a load test using production-like prompt and output lengths, and compare output quality against the baseline on your own eval set. A change that fits memory but lowers quality 3 points may be worse than buying one more GPU.

Tools to inspect memory: nvidia-smi (total used, per process), torch.cuda.memory_summary() and torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() inside Python, vLLM and TGI startup logs (they print the allocated KV cache token count, which you can compare with your formula), and Prometheus metrics for cache usage (vLLM exposes GPU cache usage percentage; verify metric names for your version).

Python, quickly checking GPU memory from code:

import torch

free, total = torch.cuda.mem_get_info()                 # bytes on current device
print(f"free {free/1e9:.1f} GB of {total/1e9:.1f} GB")   # e.g. free 76.2 GB of 85.1 GB (an 80 GiB card in decimal GB)

Kotlin and Java: the JVM has no direct CUDA memory API in the standard library. Read it by running nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.total --format=csv,noheader,nounits as a subprocess and parsing the line, or scrape the Prometheus metrics of the serving engine. Kotlin:

fun main() {
    val p = ProcessBuilder("nvidia-smi", "--query-gpu=memory.used,memory.total", "--format=csv,noheader,nounits").start()
    println(p.inputStream.bufferedReader().readText().trim())   // e.g. "41234, 81920" (MiB used, MiB total)
}

Java:

public class GpuMem {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Process p = new ProcessBuilder("nvidia-smi", "--query-gpu=memory.used,memory.total",
                "--format=csv,noheader,nounits").start();
        System.out.println(new String(p.getInputStream().readAllBytes()).trim()); // e.g. "41234, 81920"
    }
}

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: a cargo plane with a weight limit. If the plane will not take off, remove cargo (shorter contexts, fewer concurrent requests), repack it smaller (quantize), or charter a second plane (more GPUs), in roughly that order of cost.

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping straight to "add GPUs" without checking limits and KV quantization.
  • Reading nvidia-smi "memory used" as the model's need. Engines pre-allocate their pool, so it shows the configured budget, not the true usage.
  • Quantizing weights to solve a problem that is actually KV cache or activation spikes.
  • Not re-validating quality after each memory-saving change.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Why formats: 70B params x 2 bytes = 140 GB; low-bit storage (plus scales) makes it 35 to 42 GB. Real 4-bit cost is about 4.15 to 4.8 bits per weight because of group scales and zero-points.
  • Scale-and-round: scale = max|w| / 7, q = round(w / scale), w_hat = q x scale. Smaller groups isolate outliers but cost more metadata.
  • GPTQ: layer-wise post-training quantization that minimises layer output error and pushes rounding error onto remaining weights using the inverse Hessian; needs calibration data; GPU serving.
  • AWQ: finds the salient channels from activation statistics and rescales them (with a compensating inverse scale on the activations) so everything stays uniform 4-bit; calibration is lighter; GPU serving.
  • GGUF: a single-file format for llama.cpp with weights, tokenizer and metadata; quant types Q4_0 (4.5 bits), Q8_0 (8.5 bits), k-quants like Q4_K_M (about 4.8 bits average, the usual sweet spot), and imatrix-assisted I-quants for 2 to 3 bits; the home of CPU, Apple and edge inference.
  • TGI: Hugging Face's Rust+Python server with continuous batching, streaming, quantization flags and OpenAI-compatible routes; set input/total/prefill token limits from real traffic; check maintenance status (verify).
  • llama.cpp: C/C++ engine on ggml; llama-server gives an OpenAI-compatible API; -c is shared across -np slots; -ngl controls GPU offload; ideal for local and edge, not for large multi-user GPU throughput.
  • Triton: NVIDIA's general model-serving platform (model repository, dynamic batching, ensembles, gRPC/HTTP KServe v2, Prometheus) hosting TensorRT-LLM or vLLM backends; do not confuse with OpenAI Triton, the kernel language.
  • Weights memory: params x bits / 8; MoE models need total, not active, parameters in memory; training needs about 16 bytes per parameter with Adam.
  • KV cache memory: 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes x tokens; Llama 3.1 70B is 320 KiB per token at fp16, so a 128k context is about 40 GiB; use KV heads, not attention heads.
  • Budget: pool = util x GPU - weights - activations - overhead; worked example: 70B AWQ on 80 GB leaves about 30 GB, roughly 93k tokens, about 31 requests of 3k tokens; decode speed bound is bandwidth / bytes read per token.
  • Operations: diagnose by when OOM happens (startup vs load vs specific prompts); cut limits and concurrency first, quantize KV next, then weights, then add GPUs; always re-evaluate quality and load-test.
